en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 6. Jarāsuttaniddesa (The Exposition of the Discourse on Old Age)
Now he will explain the Jarā Sutta:
"Truly brief is this life;
one dies even before reaching a hundred years."
Even if one lives for a very long time,
one will still die from old age;
indeed, this life is truly short.
"Life" means vitality, stability, subsistence, maintenance, proceeding, persistence, preservation, life, and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
Furthermore, life is short and brief for two reasons:
either because its duration is limited, or because its inherent nature is limited.
How is life short due to the brevity of its duration?
In the past moment of consciousness, one lived, but does not live now, nor will one live [in the future];
in the future moment of consciousness, one will live, but does not live now, nor did one live [in the past].
In the present moment of consciousness one lives; one has not lived, nor will one live.
“Life and the individual existence, and all pleasure and pain—”
When joined with a single thought,
the moment passes swiftly.
Eighty-four thousand [moments]...
The gods remain for an eon,
yet even they do not truly live when joined with two minds.
All the aggregates that have ceased for one who is dying here, or for one who is still living, are alike.
Those who have passed away without rebirth,
those who have broken through in this very life, and those who will break through in the future;
In the interval between those [moments],
there is no disparity in their characteristics;
one who has not been produced is not born.
One lives by means of the present;
the world is dead when the mind has perished;
it exists only as a conventional designation for the ultimate truth.
Just as rivers flow according to their incline,
directed by their own impulse,
so do they roll on with an unbroken stream.
Conditioned by the six sense bases:
they have gone to non-deposition, shattered;
there is no heap remaining for the future.
Those phenomena that have arisen and persist are like a mustard seed on the point of an awl.
Of those phenomena that have arisen...
Their destruction is placed before them;
subject to dissolution, they stand unmixed with those of the past.
They come from non-appearance and,
upon dissolution, go to non-appearance; like the arising of light in the sky, they arise and pass away.
“They arise and pass away.
Thus, life is short by virtue of its limited duration.
How is life short by virtue of its inherent frailty?
Life is bound up with the in-breath; life is bound up with the out-breath; life is bound up with both the in-breath and the out-breath;
life is bound up with the great primary elements; life is bound up with physical nutriment;
life is bound up with heat; life is bound up with consciousness.
Their root is weak; their prior causes are weak; their conditions are weak; their enablers are weak;
their co-existents are weak; their associations are weak; their conascent factors are weak; and their motivators are also weak.
These are perpetually weak against one another; these are unstable against one another.
They cause one another to fall, for there is no protector among them; nor do they establish one another, and even that which produces them is not found.
“Not one among them is surpassed by another,
for all these are gandhabbas; yet these latter are more radiant than those former ones.”
"Those who were formerly known as radiant ones—
both those of the past and those of the future—
never saw one another."
Thus, because of its meager essence,
life is trifling. Moreover, compared to the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings,
the life of humans is trifling, limited, brief, momentary, fleeting, short-lived, transient, and not enduring.
Life is not long-enduring; life is short-lived—for the gods of the Thirty-three, and for the Yāma gods... [and so on].
...of the Tusita devas ...
of the Nimmānarati devas ...
of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas ...
Compared to the lifespan of the gods of the Brahma-body realm, the lifespan of human beings is short,
limited, meager, momentary, fleeting, brief, transient, not substantial, and does not endure for long.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, short is the life of humans; the world beyond must be reached. One must be awakened through wisdom; what is wholesome must be done; the holy life must be lived. There is no immortality for one who is born.
Whoever, bhikkhus, lives long, lives a hundred years or a little more.”
The lifespan of humans is short;
a wise person should not despise it.
One should live as if one's head were on fire.
There is no arrival of death for mortals.
Days and nights pass by,
and life comes to an end.
"The life of mortals wastes away,
like the water in little rills.
Alas, this life is indeed short!
"One will die even before a hundred years have passed.
Even at the stage of the *kalala*, one passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates;
even at the stage of the *abbuda*, one passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates.
In the time of the fruit-stalks, it passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates;
in the time of the dense growth, it passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates;
in the time of the shoots, it passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates.
Even as soon as it is born, it passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates;
even in the birth-chamber it passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates;
even at half a month old, it passes away, dies, disappears, and disintegrates.
Even one month old passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes;
even two months old...
even three months old...
Even after four months...
even after five months, one passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes;
even after six months...
...even one seven months old,
...even one eight months old,
...even one nine months old...
Even one ten months old...
even one a year old passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes;
even one two years old...
Even one who has been ordained for three years… even one who has been ordained for four years… even one who has been ordained for five years…
Even one who is five years old… even one who is seven years old… even one who is eight years old…
One who has been ordained for nine years... one who has been ordained for ten years...
one who has been ordained for twenty years...
Even one who is thirty years old...
even one who is forty years old...
even one who is fifty years old...
Even one who is sixty years old...
even one who is seventy years old...
even one who is eighty years old...
"Even one ninety years old passes away, dies, vanishes, and perishes;
thus, even within a hundred years, one dies.
And yet, some live beyond that."
He who lives having exceeded a hundred years lives for one year,
or he lives for two years,
or he lives for three years.
He lives for four years,
or he lives for five years …pe… or he lives for ten years.
"He lives for twenty years,
or he lives for thirty years, or he lives for forty years"—
even if he lives beyond that.
Furthermore, one dies even because of old age.
When one is aged, grown old, advanced in years, come to the final stage of life—having broken teeth, grey hair, and a balding, shaven head;
with wrinkled skin and limbs marred by spots; being bent, crooked, and leaning on a staff—one passes away even due to old age.
It dies, it vanishes, it falls apart; there is no escape from death.
"Just as ripe fruits are in constant fear of falling early, so too for mortals there is constant fear of death."
Thus for mortals who are born,
there is constant fear of death,
just as for a potter [there is fear for his unbaked pots].
Just as a vessel made of clay has breaking as its end,
so too is the life of mortals.
Both the small and the great,
both the foolish and the wise—
all go under the power of death.
All have death as their ultimate end.
For those who are overtaken by death and departing from this world to the next,
A father does not protect his son,
nor do kinsmen protect their kin; while the kinsmen look on, [death carries him away].
Behold how they lament individually;
for mortals, each one alone is led away like a bull to the slaughter.
"Thus is the world assailed by death and by old age"—
and then he dies even from old age.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Truly, this life is short;
one dies even before reaching a hundred years."
And even he who lives for a long time,
will nevertheless die through old age.
People grieve for what they cherish.
For possessions are not eternal;
seeing that this very world is subject to separation, one should not dwell in a household.
"People grieve for what they have claimed as 'mine'. Who grieves?
Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans. "Claiming as mine" refers to two kinds of claiming as mine:
[the claim of ownership regarding material things and the claim of ownership regarding views].
The intoxication of craving and the intoxication of views … [as above] … this is the intoxication of craving … [as above] … this is the intoxication of views.
People grieve for what they have clung to as "mine": they grieve when they fear its loss, they grieve while it is being lost, and they grieve once it has been lost.

They grieve when they fear the change of what they have clung to as "mine": they grieve while it is changing, and they grieve once it has changed. They become exhausted, they lament, they beat their breasts, they wail, and they fall into confusion.
Thus it is said: "People grieve for what they have clung to as 'mine'."
For there are no permanent possessions.
There are two kinds of possessions:
the possession of craving and the possession of views... [and so on]...
This is the acquisition of craving... [and so on] ...this is the acquisition of views.
The acquisition of craving is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen; it is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to change.
The acquisition of views is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to change.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Do you see, monks, that acquisition which is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and which might remain exactly as it is for all eternity?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.
I too, bhikkhus, do not see any acquisition that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that would remain exactly as it is for all eternity.”

"Acquisitions are not permanent, stable, eternal, or of an unchanging nature; they do not exist, they are not present, they are not found, they are not obtainable"—for indeed, there are no permanent acquisitions.
They perceive even what exists as being subject to separation.
When there is diversity, separation, and changeability—existing, being found, and being perceived.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Enough, Ānanda."
Do not grieve, do not lament.
Has this not been declared by me beforehand, Ānanda:
‘It is with all that is dear and beloved that change, separation, and alteration must occur’?
How could it be possible here, Ānanda,
that what is born, come to be, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate?
That is impossible.
“Because of the transformation and alteration of preceding aggregates, elements, and bases, succeeding aggregates, elements, and bases continue to arise”—
seeing that this very world exists only in separation [from a self], he does not live in a household.

"Thus" (*iti*) means: the junction of words, the connection of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequential order of words—this is what it is.
"Thus" (*iti*) means: having seen, having perceived, having weighed, having judged, having discerned, having made manifest; "among notions of 'mine'" (*mamattesu*)—thus, having seen.
He does not dwell in a village, having severed all the impediments of household life;

having severed the impediment of children and wife, having severed the impediment of relatives, having severed the impediment of friends and companions, and having severed the impediment of hoarding wealth;
having shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and gone forth from the home into homelessness, he abides in a state of possessing nothing.
"Having approached [the homeless life], one should wander alone, dwell, conduct oneself, behave, protect, maintain, and sustain oneself"— having seen this, one should not live in a household.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“People grieve for what they have claimed as ‘mine,’ for possessions are never permanent;
this very world is subject to separation.”
"Having seen this, one should not dwell in a home.
Even by death is that abandoned which a man thinks, "This is mine."
Having understood this as well, the wise one,
my follower, should not bow down out of attachment to "mine.
Even by death, that [attachment] is abandoned.

“Death” means: for those various beings, the passing away from their respective classes of beings; the state of falling away, dissolution, disappearance, death, dying, the time of death, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life-faculty.
“That” refers to what has come under the category of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
“Is abandoned” means it is abandoned, relinquished, left behind, disappears, and falls apart.
For this has also been said:
"Wealth leaves a mortal first,
or the mortal leaves it first."
Those who desire sensual pleasures possess wealth that is impermanent;
therefore, I do not grieve during a time of sorrow.
The moon rises, waxes full, and then wanes.
Having blazed forth, the sun departs;
I have understood these worldly conditions, Sattuka,
therefore I do not grieve at a time for grieving.
It is abandoned even by death.
"That which a person thinks 'this is mine'" refers to whatever has come into form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
"Person" is a designation, a common usage, a description, a name, a naming, a denomination, a linguistic expression, a syllable, a verbal utterance.
"He conceives 'it is mine'"— he conceives by means of the conceiving of craving, he conceives by means of the conceiving of views, he conceives by means of the conceiving of conceit,
he conceives by means of the conceiving of defilements, he conceives by means of the conceiving of misconduct, he conceives by means of the conceiving of application.
"He conceives by means of the conceiving of kamma-result" means that a person conceives, "This is mine.
Having understood this as well, one is wise.

"Having known this danger, having understood it, weighed it, scrutinized it, clarified it, and made it manifest as 'possessions' (*mamatta*)— having understood even this, the wise one, the steadfast one, the learned, the one possessed of wisdom, the intelligent, the one with knowledge, the one who has clarified things,
the one endowed with discernment— having understood even this,
the wise one does not incline toward possessiveness, thinking 'mine'."
"Mine-ness": there are two kinds of mine-ness—craving-mine-ness and view-mine-ness ... [as before] ...
this is craving-mine-ness ... [as before] ...
This is the measure of views.
"It is mine" refers to being devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha.
He treats the Blessed One as his own, and the Blessed One accepts that person as his own.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are hypocritical, stubborn, talkative, sycophantic, arrogant, and unconcentrated—those bhikkhus, I say, are not mine;
and those bhikkhus, I say, have departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
And they do not attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.
But those monks, bhikkhus, who are free from guile, free from chatter, steadfast, not arrogant, and well-composed—they, bhikkhus, are my monks;
and they, bhikkhus, have not departed from this Dhamma and Discipline.
And they attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Deceitful, stubborn, prattlers, and hypocritical;
arrogant, unconcentrated;
Those qualities taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One do not grow in those who are deceitful and flattering;
they grow in the wise who are free from guile and flattery.
Free from sloth and well-composed,
they indeed flourish in the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Let not my son bow down to the conceit of 'mine'.

My son, having abandoned the conceit of craving and relinquished the conceit of views, should not bow down to the conceit of "mine," should not incline toward it; he should not be prone to it, not leaning toward it, not devoted to it, and not subject to its dominance—thus:
"Let not my son bow down to the conceit of 'mine'."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Even by death that is abandoned,
which a man thinks, ‘This is mine.’”
Having understood this as well, the wise one,
my follower, should not bow down out of attachment to "mine.
Just as a meeting in a dream—
A man who has awakened does not see [the dream];
even so, one does not see a beloved person who has passed away and died.
"As gathered together as in a dream":
"Gathered," "assembled," "composed," "come together"—
this is what is meant by "as gathered together as in a dream."
"A man who has awakened does not see" means that just as a man while dreaming sees the moon,
sees the sun, sees the great ocean, sees Sineru the king of mountains, sees an elephant, sees a horse, sees a chariot,
sees a foot soldier, sees a military array, and sees delightful parks and delightful groves; [so too does he not see these upon awakening].
…he sees delightful ground, … he sees delightful lotus ponds;
having awakened, he sees nothing at all— thus,
a person who has awakened does not see.
"In this way they treat those who are beloved.
"In this way" is the application of the simile.
"They treat as beloved" means they treat as their own those people who are mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, friends, ministers, kinsmen, or blood relations.
In this way, one does not see even a beloved person who has passed away and died.
"Passed away" (peta) means dead.
"He does not see, he does not behold, he does not attain, he does not find, he does not acquire one who has passed away"—
thus, "he does not see the deceased.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Just as a person who has awakened does not see what was encountered in a dream,
so too one does not see beloved people.”
One does not see that which is deceased and passed away.
Those people whose names are thus proclaimed— whether seen or heard of— [do not exist].
"Only the name will remain of that person,
as a mere thing to be spoken of.
'I have seen him,' or 'I have heard of him'— thus people will know of him."
"Seen" refers to those things produced by eye-consciousness.
"Hear" refers to those things produced by ear-consciousness.
"Those people" refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans.
"Those people have been seen or heard of,
whose names are thus proclaimed.
"Whose" means whose— of those kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans.
"Name" means a designation, a common usage, a description, a conventional term, a name, a naming, a denomination, an expression, a phrasing, a verbalization.
It is "called" (pavuccati) in the sense that it is spoken, is uttered, is told, is recited, is explained, and is conventionally designated;
thus, "of those whose name this is called."
"Only a name will remain, as something to be described.

Whatever has become form, whatever has become feeling, whatever has become perception, whatever has become formations, and whatever has become consciousness is abandoned, relinquished, left behind, disappears, and falls apart; only a name will remain, as something to be described.
"To be told, to be spoken, to be uttered, to be illuminated,
to be expressed"— thus, "the expressible" (akkheyya) remains as a mere name for that person who has passed away.
"Of a peta" means of one who has died, passed away. "Of a jantu" means of a being,
a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a soul, a creature, a sentient being, a human, a mortal, a human being—
thus, "of a peta, a jantu."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Those people by whose names this [name] is proclaimed, whether seen or heard of— ”
"Only a name will remain,
a mere report of that person. [He abandons] sorrow,
lamentation, and stinginess.
The greedy do not abandon what they cherish as "mine";
therefore, the sages, seeing safety,
went forth having abandoned possessiveness.
"The greedy do not abandon grief, fear, and stinginess regarding what they cherish. Here,
"grief" refers to that which arises for one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or the loss of wealth, or the loss of health,
or the loss of virtue, or the loss of right view, or by some other such misfortune.

For one who is possessed of misfortune and touched by some kind of painful state, there is sorrow, grieving, the state of being grieved, inner sorrow, inner affliction, inner burning, inner torment, the consuming of the mind, mental distress, and the dart of sorrow.
Lamentation is [the state] for one touched by the loss of relatives... [and so on].
For one who is afflicted by the calamity of wrong views, or possessed of any other kind of calamity, or touched by any other state of suffering—
there is weeping, lamentation, the act of weeping, the act of lamenting, the state of having wept, the state of having lamented;
it is vain speech, confused speech, wailing, the act of wailing, and the state of having wailed.
"Stinginess" refers to the five kinds of stinginess:
stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma.
Whatever such stinginess there is—stinginess, the state of being stingy, the act of being stingy, avarice, miserliness, a harsh narrow-mindedness, and a lack of generosity of heart.
This is called stinginess.
Furthermore, stinginess regarding the aggregates is stinginess; stinginess regarding the elements is stinginess; stinginess regarding the sense bases is stinginess—this is called stinginess.
Greed is said to be craving.
It is that which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness.
Possessiveness is twofold: there are two kinds of possessiveness.
The intoxication of craving and the intoxication of views … [as above] … this is the intoxication of craving … [as above] … this is the intoxication of views.
They grieve when they fear the loss of a cherished object; they grieve while it is being lost; they grieve when it has been lost.
They grieve when they fear the change of a cherished object; they grieve while it is changing; they grieve when it has changed.
They lament when they fear the loss of a cherished object; they lament while it is being lost... [and so on].
They lament even when it has not been cut off.
They lament when they fear the change of a cherished object; they lament when it changes; they lament when it has changed.
They guard, protect, grasp, cherish, and are possessive toward a cherished object; they are stingy with it.

Regarding that which is cherished, they do not abandon sorrow; they do not abandon lamentation; they do not abandon stinginess; they do not abandon greed; they do not relinquish it, they do not discard it, they do not dispel it, they do not bring it to an end, they do not cause its disappearance.
Thus, "being greedy for what is cherished, they do not relinquish sorrow, lamentation, and stinginess.
Therefore, the sages, having abandoned possessiveness, wandered about as seers of security.
Therefore—for that reason, for that cause, for that condition, for that source—perceiving this danger, [it is said] "among those who possess self-conceit.
Therefore.
"Sages" (munayo): "muna" is said to be knowledge (ñāṇa).
That which is wisdom, understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
Endowed with that knowledge, the sages have attained sagehood (*mona*).
There are three kinds of sagehood:
Purity of body, purity of speech, purity of mind … [as above] … having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage.
“Possession” means two kinds of possession: [the internal and the external].
The appropriation of craving and the appropriation of views...
[as before] ...this is the appropriation of craving... [as before] ...this is the appropriation of views.
The sages, having abandoned the grasping of craving, having relinquished, given up, renounced,
dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the grasping of views, they moved, dwelt, conducted themselves, behaved,
maintained themselves, and sustained themselves.

"Those who see security": "Security" refers to the deathless Nibbāna—that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.

"Those who see security" means those who see security, who see refuge, who see a shelter, who see a sanctuary, who see fearlessness, who see the undecaying, who see the deathless, and who see Nibbāna.
Therefore, having abandoned possessions, the sages wandered about, seeing safety.
Thus the Blessed One said:
“Grief, lamentation, and stinginess...”
The greedy do not relinquish what they have claimed as their own;
therefore, the sages, having abandoned possessiveness, have wandered on, seeing safety.
For the bhikkhu who lives in seclusion and frequents a solitary seat,
they say that this is his harmony.
"He who does not show himself in becoming—
that bhikkhu is one who lives in withdrawal.
Those who live in withdrawal are called the seven trainees (sekha).
The Arahant is withdrawn.
For what reason are the seven trainees (sekha) said to be "those who live withdrawn"?
Because they withdraw, turn back, turn away, suppress, and restrain their minds from this and that [object].
Restraining, protecting, and guarding, they move, wander, dwell, conduct themselves, act, preserve, maintain, and sustain;
at the eye-door, drawing back, turning away, and withdrawing the mind, restraining it, suppressing it,
restraining, protecting, and guarding, they move, wander, dwell, and conduct themselves.
They turn it, they protect it, they maintain it, they sustain it;
[they direct] the mind at the ear-door …pe… the mind at the nose-door …
Drawing back, turning away,
withdrawing, restraining, and suppressing the mind at the door of the tongue… at the door of the body… at the door of the mind.
Restraining, protecting, and guarding it, they move about, wander, dwell, conduct themselves, act, preserve, maintain, and sustain it.
Just as a fowl’s feather or a strip of sinew, when thrown into a fire, shrinks back, recoils, rolls away, and does not extend forward;
even so, shrinking back, recoiling, and rolling away from this and that, they restrain, suppress, and completely arrest the mind.
Restraining, guarding, and protecting, they move about, wander, dwell, conduct themselves, proceed, preserve, maintain, sustain,
and support [themselves]; [they do so] regarding the mind at the eye-door … regarding the mind at the ear-door …
The mind at the nose-door … the mind at the tongue-door … the mind at the body-door …
At the mind-door, they move, roam, dwell, conduct themselves, behave, maintain, protect, preserve, and sustain their minds by drawing it back, turning it away, rolling it back,
restraining it, suppressing it, warding it off, guarding it, and protecting it. For that reason,
the seven trainees (sekha) are called "those who move with their minds drawn back."
"A bhikkhunī" refers to a virtuous worldling bhikkhu or a bhikkhu in training;
"a bhikkhu" refers to a bhikkhu who lives in seclusion.
"Frequenting a secluded seat" refers to that seat where they sit.

A bed, a bench, a mattress, a mat, a piece of leather, a grass-strewing, a leaf-strewing, or a straw-strewing—this seat is empty, secluded, and isolated from seeing unsuitable forms; it is empty, secluded, and isolated from hearing unsuitable sounds;
[it is empty, secluded, and isolated] from smelling unsuitable odors... from tasting unsuitable flavors... from touching unsuitable tangibles.
...it is empty, secluded, and utterly remote of the five unwholesome strands of sensual pleasure.
For one who resorts to, frequents, uses, dwells upon, devotes oneself to, and cultivates that secluded seat— it is for one so resorting that the seat is secluded.
They say that harmony belongs to him who does not display himself for existence.
"Harmony" refers to three kinds of harmony:
harmony of the group, harmony of the Dhamma, and harmony of non-rebirth.
What is concord within the Saṅgha?
Even if many bhikkhus dwell together in concord, in harmony, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of affection—
this is concord within the Saṅgha.
What is the harmony of states?
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
These converge together, find confidence, become established, and are liberated.
There is no dispute or contention regarding those phenomena—
this is the concordance of the Dhamma.
What is the concordance of non-rearising?
Even if many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue,
no deficiency or fullness is perceived in that element of nibbāna—
this is the harmony of non-rearising.
"Bhavana" refers to the state of existence (bhavana): for those in hell, hell is their state of existence; for those in the animal realm, the animal realm is their state of existence;

for those in the sphere of hungry ghosts, the sphere of hungry ghosts is their state of existence; for humans, the human world is their state of existence; and for devas, the deva world is their state of existence.
They say that harmony belongs to him who does not display a self within such states of existence.
"This is harmony; this is fitting, this is appropriate, this is suitable, this is consistent— that one who is thus concealed should not show himself in hell,
should not show himself in the animal realm, should not show himself in the sphere of hungry ghosts,
should not show himself in the human world, and should not show himself in the world of the devas."
"They say thus, they speak thus, they declare thus, they illuminate thus, they express themselves thus:
'That is harmony for him who does not display himself in becoming.
Therefore the Blessed One said:"
“For a bhikkhu who lives withdrawn and frequents a secluded seat,
they say that this is his harmony.”
“He who does not display himself for existence”—
the sage, independent in all respects,
makes neither what is dear nor what is not dear.
In him, lamentation and stinginess do not adhere,
just as water does not cling to a leaf;
the Sage is independent in every respect.
"All" refers to the twelve sense bases:

the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena. "The Sage" (muni) refers to one who has attained the state of silence.
“Mona” is said to be knowledge … [as above] … having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage (muni).
“Independent” (anissita):
there are two dependencies.
The dependence on craving and the dependence on views ... [as before] ...
this is dependence on craving ... [as before] ... this is dependence on views.

The sage, having abandoned reliance on craving and relinquished reliance on views, is independent of the eye, independent of the ear, independent of the nose, independent of the tongue, independent of the body, and independent of the mind;
independent of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
independent of family, assembly, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

the sense-sphere realm … the fine-material realm … the immaterial realm … existence in the sense sphere … existence in the fine-material realm … existence in the immaterial realm … existence with perception … existence without perception … existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception … one-constituent existence … four-constituent existence … five-constituent existence … the past … the future … the present …

Not dependent on, not clinging to, not approaching, not adhering to, not intent upon, having emerged from, departed from, and being liberated from all things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—he dwells with a mind that is free from boundaries and detached.
Thus, the sage is independent in every respect;
he makes nothing dear, nor does he make anything undear.
There are two kinds of dear things:
beings or conditioned phenomena.
Which beings are dear?
In this case, those who wish for one's welfare, well-being, comfort, and security from bondage— whether they be mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, kinsman,
or blood relative— these beings are dear.
Which formations are dear?
Pleasant forms, pleasant sounds, pleasant smells, pleasant tastes, and pleasant tangibles—
these volitional formations are dear.
As for "unpleasant," there are two kinds of unpleasant things:
Either beings or formations.
Which beings are unpleasant?
Here, those who wish you no welfare, who wish you no benefit, who wish you no comfort, who wish you no security from bondage, and who wish to deprive you of life.
These beings are unpleasant.
Which conditioned phenomena are unpleasant?
Unpleasant forms, unpleasant sounds, unpleasant odors, unpleasant tastes, and unpleasant tactile objects.
These conditioned phenomena are unlovely.
One does not make them dear, nor does one make them unlovely.
Thinking, "This being is dear to me, and these conditioned phenomena are agreeable," one does not make them dear by way of lust.

Thinking, “This being is unpleasant to me, and these formations are disagreeable,” one does not, through the influence of aversion, make, produce, generate, bring about, or cause to arise what is unpleasant— thus, one neither makes it dear nor makes it unpleasant.
In that regard, lamentation and stinginess do not adhere, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
In regard to such a person— an Arahant whose taints are exhausted—
lamentation arises when one is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by illness,
or afflicted by the loss of virtue, or afflicted by the loss of right view, or by some other such misfortune.
For one who is beset by misfortune and touched by some form of suffering, there is weeping, lamentation, the act of weeping, the act of lamenting, the state of weeping, the state of lamenting;
it is vain speech, excessive speech, wailing, the act of wailing, and the state of wailing.
As for stinginess, there are five kinds of stinginess:
Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma.
Whatever such stinginess, the act of being stingy, the state of being stingy, secrecy, meanness, harshness,
and the grip of the mind— this is called stinginess.
Moreover, stinginess regarding the aggregates is stinginess; stinginess regarding the elements is stinginess; stinginess regarding the sense bases is stinginess—this is called stinginess.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
"Leaf" refers to a lotus leaf.
"Water" refers to water.
Just as water does not smear, does not defile, and does not adhere to a lotus leaf—remaining unsmeared, undefiled, and unadhered to—
In the same way, lamentation and stinginess do not smear, besmear, or defile that person—an Arahant whose taints are destroyed;

being unsmeared, unbesmeared, and undefiled, that Arahant person is not smeared, not besmeared, and not defiled by those defilements; unsmeared, unbesmeared, and undefiled, he dwells with a mind that has gone forth, escaped, is liberated, detached, and free from boundaries.
In that state, lamentation and stinginess do not cling to him, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The sage is independent in all circumstances.”
One does not do what is dear, nor what is not dear;
lamentation and stinginess regarding that [object] do not cling,
just as water does not cling to a leaf.
Just as a drop of water does not cling to a lotus leaf,
or as water does not cling to a lotus flower,
even so the sage is not defiled.
Namely, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed:
"Just as a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
A "drop of water" refers to a small amount of water.
"Lotus" refers to a lotus leaf.
Just as a drop of water does not adhere to, cling to, or stick to a lotus leaf— being unadhered to, unclung to, and unstuck to—
so too is it "like a drop of water on a lotus."
"Just as a lotus is not smeared by water":
"lotus" refers to the lotus flower;
"water" refers to water.
Just as water does not cling to, smear upon, or adhere to a lotus flower— being unclung to, unsmeared,
and unadhered to— so too, like water on a lotus,
the sage is not smeared by that which is seen, heard, or thought.
Thus is the application of the simile.
“The Sage” (muni): “Mona” is said to be knowledge … [as before] … having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage.
There are two kinds of clinging:
the clinging of craving and the clinging of views... [as before] ...this is the clinging of craving... [as before] ...
This is the smear of views.

Having abandoned the smear of craving and relinquished the smear of views, the sage does not smear himself on what is seen, does not smear himself on what is heard, does not smear himself on what is sensed, and does not smear himself on what is cognized;
he does not smear, does not smear over, and does not smear upon them. Unsmearred, unsmeared, and unsmeared by anything, he remains so.
"Having gone forth, having escaped, being liberated, and being detached, he dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries—
thus the sage is not defiled by what is seen or heard among those who are deluded.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
Just as a drop of water does not cling to a lotus leaf,
or as water does not cling to a lotus flower,
even so the sage is not defiled.
"Namely, that which is seen, heard, or sensed"—
the one who is free from worldly attachments does not,
on account of these, form conceits regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed.
He does not seek purity through anything else,
for he neither becomes stained nor is he unstained.
The one who is free from worldly things does not conceive notions because of that— namely, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed.
“Dhonā”—cleansing—is said to be wisdom (*paññā*).
That which is wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
For what reason is wisdom called “cleansing”?
By means of that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified;
verbal misconduct … mental misconduct is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
Lust is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly cleansed, and purified;
hatred … delusion … [is likewise].
anger … ill will … hypocrisy …
... malice ...
envy ...
avarice ...
Deceit … guile … obstinacy …
Aggression … conceit … overweening pride …
Intoxication … negligence … all defilements …
All misconducts… all distresses… all fevers…
All fevers... all unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
For that reason, wisdom is called "the purifier."
Alternatively, by right view, wrong view is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and cleansed;
by right intention, wrong intention is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly washed away, and cleansed;
by right speech, wrong speech is shaken off...
By right action, wrong action is shaken off;
by right livelihood, wrong livelihood is shaken off;
by right effort, wrong effort is shaken off.
By right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is shaken off;
by right concentration, wrong concentration is shaken off;
and by right knowledge, wrong knowledge is shaken off.
By means of right liberation, wrong liberation is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
Alternatively, by means of the noble eightfold path, all defilements... all misconducts... [are shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified].
All distresses … all fevers … all torments …
All unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
The Arahant is endowed with these purifying qualities—fully endowed, fully possessed, attained, fully attained, perfected, fully perfected, and equipped.
Therefore, the Arahant is "the Purified One."
Thus, one whose passion is shaken off, whose evil is shaken off, whose defilements are shaken off, and whose fevers are shaken off is called "shaken off" (dhona).
Being shaken off, he does not conceive on account of that— namely, what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized.

One does not conceive of what is seen; one does not conceive in regard to what is seen; one does not conceive from what is seen; one does not conceive, "It is seen by me. One does not conceive of what is heard;
one does not conceive in regard to what is heard; one does not conceive from what is heard; one does not conceive, "It is heard by me. One does not conceive of what is sensed;
one does not conceive in regard to what is sensed; one does not conceive from what is sensed; one does not conceive, "It is sensed by me."
One does not conceive of what is cognized; one does not conceive in what is cognized; one does not conceive from what is cognized;
one does not conceive, "This is mine. For this was also said by the Blessed One: "Monks, 'I am' is a conceiving; 'This I am' is a conceiving; 'I shall be' is a conceiving."
‘I shall exist’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be possessed of form’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be formless’—this is a conceit;
‘I shall be percipient’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be non-percipient’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’—this is a conceit.
“Conceiving, monks, is a disease; conceiving is a tumor; conceiving is an arrow; conceiving is a calamity.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall dwell with a mind free from conceiving.
For one who is detached does not conceive on account of that which is seen, heard, or sensed among those things.”
"He does not seek purity by another means":
the one who has shaken off defilements (*dhona*) seeks no path to purification other than through wrong practice, a non-leading path;
that is, other than the foundations of mindfulness, other than the right efforts, other than the bases of psychic power, other than the faculties, and other than the powers.

Apart from the factors of enlightenment, one does not desire, approve of, long for, yearn for, or crave purification, complete purification, total purification, liberation, deliverance, or absolute deliverance by means of the Noble Eightfold Path;
thus, "one does not seek purification through anything else."
"For he neither lusts nor is he dispassionate.
All foolish worldlings lust; from the "good worldling" upward, the seven types of trainees are dispassionate;
the Arahant neither lusts nor is he dispassionate.

He is dispassionate because of the destruction of lust, being free from lust; because of the destruction of hatred, being free from hatred; because of the destruction of delusion, being free from delusion.
He has completed his residence [in the training], fulfilled the practice... [as before] ...the cycle of birth, aging, and death;
for him there is no further becoming—indeed, he neither clings nor is he dispassionate.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The wise man does not conceive pride on account of that which is seen, heard, or thought.”
One does not seek purity through anything else,
for such a one neither becomes stained nor is freed from stain.
Thus ends the sixth exposition, the Discourse on Old Age.
